content: Acute toxoplasma retinochoroiditis is a condition that can cause temporary ocular discomfort and has the potential to result in permanent visual loss. The primary goal of antibiotic treatment in this condition is to reduce the risk of permanent visual impairment, prevent recurrent episodes of retinochoroiditis, and alleviate the severity and duration of acute symptoms. However, there is uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of antibiotic therapy in achieving these outcomes. To address this uncertainty, a systematic review was conducted to compare the effects of antibiotic treatment versus placebo or no treatment for toxoplasma retinochoroiditis. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated any antibiotic known to be active against Toxoplasma gondii. Trials involving immunocompromised participants were excluded. Antibiotics could be administered via oral, intramuscular, intravenous, or intravitreal routes. The primary outcomes assessed were visual acuity at least three months after treatment and the risk of recurrent retinochoroiditis. Secondary outcomes included improvement in intraocular inflammation, lesion size, and adverse events. The review identified four RCTs involving a total of 268 participants. In all four studies, antibiotics were administered orally. One study conducted in Brazil compared trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole over 20 months to no treatment. This study included both adults and children and was judged to have a high risk of performance, detection, and attrition bias. The other three studies compared antibiotic treatment to placebo. These studies were assessed as having a mixture of low or unclear risk of bias due to poor reporting. One study in the United States evaluated pyrimethamine-trisulfapyrimidine for eight weeks in adults. Another study in the United Kingdom assessed pyrimethamine for four weeks in both children and adults. A third study in Brazil investigated trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 12 months in adults. In the latter study, all participants initially received antibiotics for 45 days to treat active retinochoroiditis before being randomized to either trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or placebo. Only the Brazilian study of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole over 12 months, in participants with healed lesions, reported on the effect of treatment on visual acuity. The results suggested that antibiotic treatment may not significantly improve visual acuity compared to placebo at one year (mean difference -1.00 letters, 95% confidence interval [CI] -7.93 to 5.93 letters; 93 participants; low-quality evidence). Antibiotic treatment was found to probably reduce the risk of recurrent retinochoroiditis compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.26, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.63; 227 participants; 3 studies; I² = 0%; moderate-quality evidence). This effect was observed for both acute and chronic retinochoroiditis. The UK study of pyrimethamine for four weeks reported a possible improvement in intraocular inflammation in treated participants compared to controls (RR 1.76, 95% CI 0.98 to 3.19; 29 participants; low-quality evidence). The Brazilian study of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 12 months noted that inflammation severity was higher in the placebo group compared to the antibiotic-treated group, but no further details were provided. In the US study of pyrimethamine-trisulfapyrimidine for eight weeks, intraocular inflammation had nearly resolved in all participants by the end of the study. However, it is important to note that all participants in this study also received steroid treatment. Adverse events were reported in two studies (the UK and US studies) and were more common in participants receiving antibiotics. These adverse events included reductions in hemoglobin, leukocyte, and platelet counts, as well as nausea, loss of appetite, rash, and joint pain (arthralgia). In conclusion, antibiotic treatment likely reduces the risk of recurrent toxoplasma retinochoroiditis. However, there is currently no strong evidence to suggest that this reduction in recurrence translates into improved visual outcomes. It is important to note that the absence of evidence for an effect does not equate to evidence of no effect. Further well-designed trials involving individuals with acute and chronic toxoplasma retinochoroiditis affecting any part of the retina are needed to better understand the impact of antibiotic treatment on visual outcomes.
